q: A stationary wave is the resultant wave by the superposition of two waves of the same type having equal amplitudes and velocities traveling in _____ directions.
e: A stationary wave needs two waves of the same type, equal amplitude and speed, travelling opposite ways. A stationary wave is the resultant wave by the superposition of two waves of the same type having equal amplitudes and velocities traveling in opposite directions. The same or perpendicular is not this quantity.

q: Unlike progressive waves, stationary waves do not spread out but remain in the region in which they are produced, so they are also called _____ waves.
e: A stationary wave stays in one region, so it is also called a standing wave. Unlike progressive waves, stationary waves do not spread out but remain in the region in which they are produced, so they are also called standing waves. Do not trade standing for traveling or transverse.

q: When two or more waves pass the same point, the resultant wave at that point is the sum of the individual waves. This is called the principle of _____
e: Superposition: the resultant at a point is the sum of the individual displacements. When two or more waves pass the same point, the resultant wave at that point is the sum of the individual waves. This is called the principle of superposition. Interference or reflection is not this quantity.

q: In a stationary wave, the points that are always stationary are called _____
e: Nodes never move. They sit half a wavelength apart. In a stationary wave, the points that are always stationary are called nodes. Antinodes or crests is not this quantity.

q: In a stationary wave, the points between nodes that vibrate with the largest amplitude are called _____
e: Antinodes are the peaks of vibration, midway between nodes. In a stationary wave, the points between nodes that vibrate with the largest amplitude are called antinodes. Do not trade antinodes for nodes or troughs.

q: The distance between two successive nodes (or) antinodes in a stationary wave is equal to _____
e: Antinodes are the peaks of vibration, midway between nodes. The distance between two successive nodes (or) antinodes in a stationary wave is equal to (λ)/(2). λ or (λ)/(4) is a different relation from (λ)/(2).

q: The distance from a node to the nearest antinode in a stationary wave is equal to _____
e: From a node to the next antinode is λ/4. The distance from a node to the nearest antinode in a stationary wave is equal to (λ)/(4). (λ)/(2) or λ is a different relation from (λ)/(4).

q: If the resultant wave has a larger amplitude than that of individual waves, this is said to be _____ interference.
e: Interference needs coherent waves. Bright fringes are constructive; dark fringes are destructive. If the resultant wave has a larger amplitude than that of individual waves, this is said to be constructive interference. Do not trade constructive for destructive or neutral.

q: If the resultant wave has zero amplitude, this is said to be _____ interference.
e: Interference needs coherent waves. Bright fringes are constructive; dark fringes are destructive. If the resultant wave has zero amplitude, this is said to be destructive interference. Constructive or partial is not this quantity.

q: Sound waves which travel in air when we speak are examples of _____ waves.
e: Speech in air is a progressive wave, not a standing wave. Sound waves which travel in air when we speak are examples of progressive waves. Stationary or longitudinal only is not this quantity.
